1-getting-started/5-yuuko-bindings-(part.title: 5 - Yuuko Bindings (Part 2)
1-getting-started/5-yuuko-bindings-(part.description:
Yuuko Bindings solves the fundamental problem of cross-device computing: "My files are on Device A, but I'm on Device B. Where are they now?"Specifically, we want to do this without just using relative filepaths.// Original path on Windows Desktop:
"C:\Users\Alice\Music\Playlist\songName.mp3" // On Android phone becomes:
"/storage/emulated/0/Music/Playlist/songNameAlt.mp3" // On Linux laptop becomes:
"/home/alice/Music/Playlist/song."
Yuuko Bindings gives all these paths and even files the same UUID: "A3F8C9D2E1B7"
Hash-Based UUID Generation:
// Uses xxHash64 on "DeviceName|FullPath"
// "Desktop-PC|C:\Users\Alice\Music" → "A3F8C9D2E1B7"
xxHash64 is fast, collision-resistant, and portable across platforms.
Three-Tier Resolution:
public async Task<string?> GetDirectoryById(string directoryId)
{ // 1. Try original path on original device if (binding.Ref.OriginalDevice == ThisDeviceId && Directory.Exists(binding.Ref.FullPath)) return binding.Ref.FullPath; // Fast path // 2. Try previously resolved path (verified) if (binding.Resolution?.Verified == true && Directory.Exists(binding.Resolution.ResolvedPath)) return binding.Resolution.ResolvedPath; // Cached // 3. Resolve/create with fallback var resolvedPath = ResolveDirectory(binding, defaultFolder); // Creates local version if needed
} Intelligent Fallback Creation:
// If "C:\Users\Alice\Music" doesn't exist on this device:
// Creates: "~/Documents/XRUIOS/A3F8C9D2E1B7/"
// And remembers this resolution
// App code NEVER cares about actual paths:
var songPath = await dirManager.GetDirectoryById("A3F8C9D2E1B7");
// Works on ANY device without code changes Save project on Windows desktop
Open on Android tablet → files are there (copied/created locally)
Edit on Linux laptop → same UUID, different physical path
Sync changes back to original device when available
// Device B can't reach Device A's original path?
// No problem: uses last-known resolution
// When Device A comes back online: automatic reconciliation
This is where it gets interesting. [Device A] ←→ [PhotonStars Network] ←→ [Device B] ↑ [Device C, D, E...]
public class PhotonStarNetwork
{ // 1. DECENTRALIZED DISCOVERY public Task<List<StarNode>> DiscoverNodes() { // Not centralized servers, but peer-to-peer mesh // Each device is a "star" in the constellation } // 2. BINDING SYNCHRONIZATION public Task SyncBindings(StarNode targetNode) { // "Hey Device B, here are my directory bindings" // Device B merges them intelligently // Conflict resolution: timestamps, user preference } // 3. FEDERATED RESOLUTION public Task<string> FederatedResolve(string uuid) { // "Who has directory A3F8C9D2E1B7?" // Network consensus: "Device A has it at path X" // Or: "Multiple devices have it, here are options" } // 4. DYNAMIC REPLICATION public Task ReplicateIfHot(string uuid) { // If many devices request same directory // Automatically replicate to nearby nodes // Like BitTorrent for directories }
}
Kirito's NerveGear (Device A) ←→ Akihiko's Server (Network Hub) ←→ Asuna's AmuSphere (Device B)Yuuko bindings are the item/equipment database that persists across logout/login (device changes).App → Local File Path → ERROR (not on this device)
App → UUID → Local Cache → (optional) Network Fetch
App → UUID → Local Cache → Network Query → ↓
[10 nearby devices respond with their paths/sync status] ↓
Choose fastest/most recent → Stream/Sync
Apps need to reference files across different devices, but file paths change between computers. What works on your dev machine breaks on someone else's. The Yuuko Protocol solves this by creating device-independent identifiers for directories that work everywhere.public readonly struct DirectoryRef
This is where the magic happens. When you give it a path like C:\Users\Walker\Music, it:
Takes the full absolute path
Combines it with the device name (Environment.MachineName)
Runs it through xxHash64 with seed "YUUKO"
Outputs a 16-character hex ID (like 3F2A8B91C6D4E507)
This ID is the same on every device that has the same path structure. No central server needed!public sealed class DirectoryBinding
Each binding stores:
Ref - The original reference (path + device)
Resolution - Where it actually exists NOW on this device
Think of it like a phonebook: you look up someone by name (UUID) to find their current address (resolved path).public string ResolveDirectory(DirectoryBinding binding, string? defaultFolder = null)
When resolving a directory:
Check if original path exists → use it directly
If not, create fallback → MyDocuments/XRUIOS/{UUID}
Save the resolution for next time
This means if you move a folder, the system adapts without breaking references.if (binding.Ref.OriginalDevice == ThisDeviceId && Directory.Exists(binding.Ref.FullPath)) return binding.Ref.FullPath;
If the current device is the original one AND the path still exists, use it. Otherwise, resolve locally. This lets you:
Share directory references between devices
Each device resolves to its own local copy
No manual path fixing needed
The Media class wraps all this for actual file access:public static async Task<ResolvedMedia> GetFile(string directoryUuid, string fileName)
It:
Takes a directory UUID + filename
Resolves the directory path
Validates the file exists
Returns full metadata
public record Handle
This is genius—it lets apps be referenced in multiple ways:
Desktop - Running app window ID
LocalApp - Installed app name
YuukoApp - Cross-platform app definition
BinaryData - Ad-hoc app bytes
DirectoryRef - App stored in a directory No Central Server - Completely peer-to-peer ID generation
Collision Resistant - xxHash64 with seed + device + path = practically unique
Self-Healing - If paths move, it creates fallbacks
Security Built In - Uses Pariah's encryption everywhere
Simple API - GetFile(uuid, filename) just works
// On Device A
var (uuid, path) = await manager.GetOrCreateDirectory(@"C:\Music"); // Share just the UUID with Device B
// On Device B
var file = await Media.GetFile(uuid, "song.mp3");
// It just works, even if music is in D:\Songs on Device B!
See? It's elegant! You should be proud of this, dummy! Crosses arms smugly.

2-development-plans/dogma-i-crdt.html.title: DOGMA I - CRDT
2-development-plans/dogma-i-crdt.html.description:
A sync layer of the system. ✓ Best for: Real-time collaboration, offline-first ✓ Pros: Automatic conflict resolution, no central server needed ✓ Cons: Complex implementation, larger sync payloads ✓ Use: Device state, UI layouts, document editing Example: Automerge, Yjs, Delta-CRDT
This is the "CRDT System — Realtime UI and States" stage from 1 - Welcome. It's what makes UI layouts and live sensor/tracking state update across devices with no central server and no manual conflict resolution. Replication messages ride the per-peer encrypted session, AKA CRDT deltas are just payloads inside AES-256-GCM envelopes. A document holds named text fields ("labels"). A device shares it with ShareAsync; every later change is sent by itself. Devices that connect compare notes and swap exactly what each is missing, so a device that was away catches up (and so do devices it never met directly). A periodic comparison is the safety net if a single message is ever lost. There is no "newest wins": merging gives the same result in any order, so nothing is lost. (The first draft compared wall clocks; clocks differ between devices, and it would have thrown edits away.) Only the device that made a document may remove it (configurable). A removed document cannot come back when devices compare notes. Anything arriving from the network is checked first: bounded names and counts, valid updates only. Junk is refused, never a crash.
The DOGMAs: DOGMA I - CRDT · DOGMA II - Operational Transformation · DOGMA III - Event Sourcing · DOGMA IV - Merkle DAG · DOGMA V - The Holy Mother · DOGMA VI - The Cogitarium · DOGMA VII - The Audit Log index

2-development-plans/dogma-ii-operational.title: DOGMA II - Operational Transformation
2-development-plans/dogma-ii-operational.description:
A sync layer of the system. ✓ Best for: Text/code collaboration, Google Docs-style ✓ Pros: Mature, efficient for text ✓ Cons: Requires central server, complex algorithms ✓ Use: Collaborative text editing, shared scripts
The "Operational Transformation Handler" stage from 1 - Welcome. Where DOGMA I - CRDT handles free form state, OT is the specialist for ordered text/code AKA collaborative editing of documents and shared scripts, handling concurrent operations so different machines can work with the samel fiels. OT classically wants a central authority to order operations; in a peer-to-peer Yuuko mesh that role can be pinned to whichever node "owns" the document (via the handshake identity), rather than a global server. Operations travel as encrypted payloads over the per peer session. Uses a custom OT library to handle a few aspects The owner of a document is the single authority that puts edits in order, as described above. Everyone else sends an edit to the owner, which transforms it over what it accepted meanwhile, applies it, and sends the result to every device that joined. Edits are sets of "keep N / insert text / delete N". Two edits made at the same time are transformed so each still means the same thing after the other has happened; both devices end with the same text. This is checked on tens of thousands of random cases and thousands of simulated sessions with messages arriving in random orders. A device that missed messages, or was away, asks the owner for what it missed when it reconnects, and keeps the edits it made meanwhile. writers: limits who may edit; anyone else's edit is refused and their text goes back to the owner's. Only the owner can order edits, so an "edit from the owner" sent by anyone else is ignored. An edit that would cut an emoji in half is refused (JSON cannot carry half of one, which would corrupt the text on the way). Limits: if the owner is offline nobody's edits are confirmed (they are kept and sent later; there is no election of a new owner); a document is at most 200,000 characters (For larger you should chunk the data); positions count UTF-16 units.

2-development-plans/dogma-iii-event-sour.title: DOGMA III - Event Sourcing
2-development-plans/dogma-iii-event-sour.description:
A sync layer of the system. ✓ Best for: Audit trails, complex business logic ✓ Pros: Full history, replayability, debugging ✓ Cons: Storage intensive, complex queries ✓ Use: Trust changes, permissions, system events
The "Event Sourcing — Trust and Permissions" stage from 1 - Welcome.
Trust and permission changes are an append-only, signed log — every change is a Dilithium5-signed event, so history is tamper evident and replayable. This is the substrate for trust-based sync visibility: a peer's current trust level is a fold over its event history, bound to the Kyber identity proven at handshake.This ensures that tampering such a file becomes a harder task for those with malicious intent while also being able to handle sync errors. Pairs naturally with the handshake's admission gate with the banned list being the simplest projection; graded trust levels are richer projections over the same event stream. Events replicate as encrypted payloads over the per-peer session.

2-development-plans/dogma-iv-merkle-dag..title: DOGMA IV - Merkle DAG
2-development-plans/dogma-iv-merkle-dag..description:
A sync layer of the system. ✓ Best for: File sync, version history ✓ Pros: Proven, efficient, content-addressed ✓ Cons: Merge conflicts require manual resolution ✓ Use: Files, settings, asset libraries
The "Git Style DAG + Keeper Of Tomes" stage from 1 - Welcome.
Files and assets are content-addressed with identical content hashes to the same node regardless of device, which is a perfect fit with Yuuko Bindings (UUID per directory) and Keeper of Tomes for albums/songs/app directories. "Replicate if hot" (PhotonStars) is the DAG spreading popular content to nearby nodes, BitTorrent-style. Content addressing means dedup + verifiable integrity for free; the handshake/session already guarantees the transport is authenticated and encrypted.
Merges that genuinely conflict fall back to manual resolution (or branch), unlike the auto-merging DOGMA I - CRDT. A file is cut in 256 KB chunks and its hash is the hash of its chunk hashes, so the same content has the same hash on every device. A folder has one hash too. A sync asks for the other device's list of files, compares it with its own and with what both devices agreed on last time, and downloads only what changed. A download that stops half way carries on where it stopped the next time it is asked to, and the developer is the one who asks (DAG.ResumeFolder). A file only one side changed follows that side. A deleted file goes to .yuuko/trash. If both sides changed the same file, the newest wins on both devices and the other is kept next to it as name (conflict 1a2b3c4d).ext, so nothing is lost and both devices end up the same. Devices tell each other when a folder changed (BroadcastUpdate) and sync by themselves (DAG.AutoSync), also when a listed device connects. Lots of notices at once become one sync. Safety: a device only gets files from folders it is listed for, only files that are in the folder's own list, and a path another device sends is never used as it is (nothing that climbs out of the folder, nothing in .yuuko, nothing through a shortcut). A missing folder is an error and a sync that would delete nearly everything refuses (DAG.AllowMassDelete). Limits: files only (empty folders aren't kept), no shortcuts or symlinks, no limit on files in a folder or on the size of a file unless you set DAG.MaxFiles / DAG.MaxFileBytes (the list of files is asked for a page at a time), one agreed state per folder (not per device), and the inside of a file is never merged. The first sync of a big folder reads every file once to hash it using Notary, which may take a little.

2-development-plans/dogma-v-the-holy-mot.title: DOGMA V - The Holy Mother
2-development-plans/dogma-v-the-holy-mot.description:
An orchestration layer of the system. ✓ Best for: App Handling, WebRTC/Facade/Etc. ✓ Pros: Simple to setup any service on another device ✓ Cons: Complexity can become big if implemented wrong ✓ Use: Services
The "Orchestration Layer" stage from 1 - Welcome.Services are specialized datapoints created with the intent of allowing a node to easily setup and connect with a specific protocol or pipeline to another machine. Nodes show their service capabilities while handling automatic setup, encryption and an easy to use pipe for the data. Services still must be prepared to a user in the way a Replicant Service or OpenClaw "app" is. Services may block certain apps from running, independent of the Yuuko Protocol system. The app side looks like: HolyMother.Start(); // once, after Identity.CreateNode // read var Apps = await HolyMother.GetApps("pc"); // everything installed on the pc var Open = await HolyMother.GetRunning("pc"); // only what is open right now // update await HolyMother.StartApp("pc", Apps[0].ID); await HolyMother.StopApp("pc", Apps[0].ID); Where the list comes from: Steam: every library listed in libraryfolders.vdf (Steam's own redistributables and Proton are left out). Games start through steam://rungameid/. WalkerWorks: one folder per app in HolyMother.WalkerWorksDirectory, the app is the file named like the folder (Name.exe, Name.xur, or Name on Linux). The apps menu: Start Menu shortcuts on Windows, .desktop files (system, user, Flatpak, Snap) on Linux. Safety: Other devices send an app ID, never a command, so they can only start what this device listed itself. Where the app is on disk is never sent. HolyMother.Allow = (Device, Action) => ... is asked before every start or stop (Action is "start" or "stop"). Say no to block it. Stopping asks the app to close, and ends it after 2 seconds if it doesn't. It matches by program, so it closes every copy of that program. A Start Menu shortcut that has arguments (it runs through powershell, cmd or a browser) and a Linux entry that runs through flatpak, snap or env can be started but not stopped, because we can't tell which process is theirs. App icons. Ask for a picture by app name, ID or path, one or a list:var Icon = await HolyMother.GetIcon("pc", "Spotify"); // one var Icons = await HolyMother.GetIcons("pc", new[] { "Spotify", "Steam", Id }); // a list (queued, asked for in batches) var Mine = HolyMother.LocalIcon("Spotify"); // this device A picture is a PNG (taken out of the program on Windows, the icon file on Linux, which can also be an SVG). Lists are queued: one request at a time in the order they came, and a long list is asked for in batches, so the answers always fit in a command. Apps with no picture are left out. Another device can only ask about apps this device listed, so a path only works if it is the path of one of them (it can't be used to look at other files).ToDo (Maybe): apps that aren't Start Menu shortcuts (Microsoft Store apps), and the Service / Service Config idea above.

A Seven Stage Protocol Handling Decentralized Sync and Communication Yuuko Protocol is a decentralized protocol created for the XRUIOS; it handles a multitude of datastreams like files, realtime data, messages and even videos alongside syncing. Cross Platform • Internet, Wifi Direct or Wired • Post Quantum Computing Resistant • No BS
New? Read 1 - What Is Yuuko Protocol, then 3 - Setting Up A Project to get a device running and 2 - Quickstart to use it

Made for the SCCN: signed streams passed along a mesh of nearby devices, strangers and all WebRTC + Facade (WIP) Based Interaction And Video Streaming (planned)
Event Sourcing - Trust and Permissions (planned; the signed, tamper-evident audit log is the simple version and is built, DOGMA VII - The Audit Log)
CRDT System - Realtime UI and States (built, any size and any number of documents, DOGMA I - CRDT)
Git Style System - File and Assets (built, any number of files and any size, and it carries on where it stopped, DOGMA IV - Merkle DAG) AES-256-GCM for request/response payloads Hard for third-party processes to inject or read traffic Designed for local-first scenarios (desktop apps ↔ local LLMs ↔ tools ↔ services) No central server required beyond the machine itself
Every other number, how it was measured and what was left out: 6 - Speed and Numbers. The .NET 8 SDK
Pariah Cybersecurity, which is free and open source on our Github. Its DLL and the Eclipse ones it works with are in the libs folder of the repo, so there is nothing to install Zenoh's native library, which the build downloads for you the first time (about 15 MB)

Zenoh C# Based API Created Eclipse-Secured Handshake + Per-Peer Encrypted Sessions (Kyber-1024 + Dilithium5 + AES-256-GCM) Multiplexed Lanes (parallel encrypted requests per peer) Connected Endpoints Handler CRDT Handler (any size, any number) Operational Transformation Handler Event Sourcing Handler (the audit log, signed and kept by other devices, is the simple version) Git Style DAG + Keeper Of Tomes (any number of files, any size, carries on where it stopped) Service Handler (The Holy Mother: apps) Trust Based Sync Visibility Easy BLE/Wifi Handling (Wi-Fi and LAN work; forming a Wi-Fi Direct group or a Bluetooth link is the app's job) P2P Mesh (Secure): the Cogitarium, strangers with Nearby, and paired devices find each other again with Reconnect Signed, tamper-evident Audit Log that other devices keep the head of

1-getting-started/1-what-is-yuuko-protoc.title: 1 - What Is Yuuko Protocol
1-getting-started/1-what-is-yuuko-protoc.description:
Yuuko Protocol is a decentralized focused, topic-based pub/sub messaging protocol for a lot of the projects being worked on at Walker Industries! As an example, it's what:
Allows different devices to speak to each other like an IoT
Replicates a Nintendo Streetpass Style experience on our headsets, handhelds and other devices
Drives the meshnet aspect of networking between headsets when in a crowd so worldscale XR still works
Sends face tracking data from a module to a computer/VRChat
Shares what apps exist and are being ran on a device
Built up off Zenoh, it has high speed capability and uses a number of security measures to help protect against bad actors.Within Yuuko Protocol exists several key systems built around being as easy to use as possible.
SimpleCRDT - Handles editing/merging the same document between different devices (CRDT)
OpTransform - Handles editing the same text/value between devices (Operational Transform)
DAG - Handles syncing folders between devices (MerkleDAG)
Cogitarium - Handles meshent style sharing between devices + Streetpass
Holy Mother - Handles viewing what apps exist on other devices and turning them on/off (Will later handle screen sharing as well)
There are two broker backends behind one interface: YuukoBroker and LocalBroker. LocalBroker is best for experiments and tests whereas Yuuko is what should be shipped with.Named after the GOAT Yuuko.

1-getting-started/6-speed-and-numbers.ht.title: 6 - Speed and Numbers
1-getting-started/6-speed-and-numbers.ht.description: How long things take and how fast they go, measured. Every number on this page comes from one run of a larger benchmark (Release build) on the machine below, so expect them to move a little from run to run: where it matters the page gives the middle of many runs and the slowest 1 in 20. That benchmark is kept outside the repo; dotnet run -c Release --project YuukoSandbox -- bench in the repo measures the first few rows yourself (the handshake, a question to a connected device, many at once, and raw AES-256-GCM). Machine: AMD64 Family 23 Model 113 Stepping 0, AuthenticAMD, 8 logical cores, 15.9 GB memory Microsoft Windows 10.0.19045, .NET 8.0.31 Date: 2026-11-12 The crypto is cheap, except signing. A Kyber-1024 key operation is about a millisecond and verifying a Dilithium5 signature is about half a millisecond. Signing is slower and uneven: the middle is 2.5 ms for a small message but 1 in 20 takes 14 ms. That is why a handshake is 5 ms, and why signing every audit entry costs more than keying it. Making a whole identity (both key pairs) is about 5 ms and happens once.Connecting is a one-time cost. The 5 ms handshake is Kyber, Dilithium5 and a throw-away key for forward secrecy. After it, asking a connected device something takes 40 µs because the encryption on an open session is fast: AES-256-GCM does about 300 MB/s on large messages (small messages are slower per byte, because each one has a fixed cost).Big commands are limited by encrypting and copying them, not by the protocol. A 1 MB command takes 21 ms in-process (96 MB/s counting both directions). Over real Zenoh it is 47 ms: the extra is the socket.Shared documents are quick for edits and fine for big ones. An edit reaches the other device in under 3 ms in the middle. A 10 MB document takes 0.3 s in pieces of 500 KB (33 MB/s). Three hundred small documents go out at about 400 a second, and a device that was away compares notes in pages of about 200 KB and gets 14 MB of documents in under a second.Folders cost most per file, not per byte. A thousand small files is 225 files a second, and 4,100 is 140 a second: each file is its own request, its own hash and its own write. One big file is faster per byte (a 10 MB file takes 0.14 s and a 100 MB file 1.1 s, about 80–100 MB/s) but each 256 KB piece is asked for and answered one after the other, so it is limited by the round trip, not the disk. That means over a real network you add about one round trip per piece: 40 pieces for 10 MB and 400 for 100 MB (an estimate from the arithmetic, not a measurement: with a 20 ms round trip that is roughly +0.8 s and +8 s). Hashing a file alone runs at 1,400 MB/s from the cache, and looking at a folder of 4,100 files for the first time takes 3.4 s.The Cogitarium sends each piece to 10 devices and they pass it on. A 10 KB piece reaches all 30 devices in 16 ms; a 100 KB piece in 78 ms; a 512 KB piece in 410 ms. A steady stream of 100 KB pieces goes at about 20 a second (2 MB/s to every device) with none missed, because the source sends each piece to its 10 first devices before the next one.The audit log is as fast as the disk. Each entry is flushed to disk before Append returns, which is the 4 ms. Checking a keyed log runs at about 100,000 entries a second; checking a signed log is 1,750 a second because every signature is verified.See also 3 - Setting Up A Project and 1 - Security Overview.

2-development-plans/dogma-vi-the-cogitar.title: DOGMA VI - The Cogitarium
2-development-plans/dogma-vi-the-cogitar.description:
A distribution layer of the system, made specifically for the SCCN, with a Streetpass model. ✓ Best for: Live streams to many nearby devices (the SCCN's Gaussian splats), Streetpass ✓ Pros: The source only talks to a few devices, every piece is signed, strangers can't change what they pass on ✓ Cons: Same network only, a crowd of fake devices is hard to tell from a real one ✓ Use: Live streams, shared logs, who passed by
The "Nintendo Streetpass style communication" feature from 1 - Welcome, and the Collective Distribution part of the SCCN (Streaming Gaussian Splatting for High-Density AR).Devices in the same chunk (an area) form a mesh. The source signs every piece and sends it to its best few neighbours, and each of them checks it and passes it to their own best few, so with 1000 devices in a room the source only talks to 10. A device that changes a piece fails the signature at the next device and is distrusted. Who gets pieces first comes from a rank (wifi, battery and how many neighbours distrust a device), and the devices also rate the main devices, with a receipt the source can check, so a group that lies is left out and the source bounces around its mains until the most devices are green. A normal Yuuko group refuses devices it doesn't know. Nearby opens a second node that lets strangers in, with only the stream commands allowed, and puts the Cogitarium on it. Not every device has to use the mesh: SetRoute lets a device get a chunk straight from the source (the internet) instead. It carries bytes you give it, acting as a transport layer.
Every call is in 8 - Collective Distribution. Paired devices that were turned off find each other again with Reconnect (2 - Identity).

2-development-plans/dogma-vii-the-audit-.title: DOGMA VII - The Audit Log
2-development-plans/dogma-vii-the-audit-.description:
A record layer of the system. ✓ Best for: Knowing what a device decided, and proving nobody rewrote it ✓ Pros: Append-only, tamper-evident, can be opened read-only while it is being written ✓ Cons: It only compares heads, it doesn't replicate the entries, and a device nobody watched can be cut off unnoticed ✓ Use: Who connected, who was refused, who was banned, which pairing windows were opened
The simple, local version of the "Event Sourcing — Trust and Permissions" stage from 1 - Welcome; DOGMA III - Event Sourcing is the richer, signed, replicated one that trust levels will be built on.Each entry contains the hash of the entry before it, so changing, removing, adding or reordering one breaks the chain from that point and Verify() names the first bad entry. With a key the hashes are HMACs, so someone who knows the format still can't rewrite history. Use a key for anything that matters, and keep it out of the same folder as the log. Only one writer can have a log open, but a read-only view works while the writer is running. Refused connections can come from anybody, so repeats of the same (who, why) within a minute are counted into one entry. A log can be signed by the device (AuditLog.Open(path, key, signer)), so someone who only holds the key can't forge one, and the device can send its newest entry to the devices it is connected to (AnchorTo) who keep it with an AuditWitness: VerifyWithWitnessesAsync then catches entries cut off the end or a log written again. The entries themselves aren't copied, only their head.
Every kind it records and every limit is in 9 - Audit Log. See also 1 - Security Overview.

3-reference/6-folder-sync.html.description:
DAG (DOGMA IV). The same folder on every device that shares it. Only what changed is sent, a download that stops carries on where it stopped the next time you sync, and nothing is put in place until it is checked.DAG.cs is the encrypted repository of the folders this device shares (the CRUD part), DAG.Sync.cs is the sync.What SyncFolder gives back (SyncResult): Downloaded, Deleted, Conflicts (list of paths), Errors (list), AlreadyInSync, LocalChanges (we have things they don't).Settings and events:The repository calls (yours): InitializeRepoFile, SetupRepo, CreateNewEntry, GetAllEntries, GetSpecificEntry, GetSpecificEntryByDirectoryPath, UpdateVariable, UpdateVariableByDirectoryPath, DeleteVariable, DeleteVariableByDirectoryPath, ReturnIfFolderExists. ShareFolder, JoinFolder and StopSharing use them for you.//On the pc
var RepoKey = new SecureData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("the repository password"));
await DAG.Start(RepoKey); var Folder = await DAG.ShareFolder(@"D:\Movies", new List<string> { "phone" }); //these are the devices allowed to have it
Console.WriteLine(Folder.UUID); //give this to the phone: type it, show it, or send it in a command
//On the phone
await DAG.Start(RepoKey2); await DAG.JoinFolder(UUIDFromThePc, "/storage/Movies", new List<string> { "pc" }); DAG.Progress += (UUID, Path, Done, Total) => Console.WriteLine($"{Path}: {Done * 100 / Total}%"); var Result = await DAG.SyncFolder("pc", UUIDFromThePc);
Console.WriteLine($"{Result.Downloaded} files, {Result.Deleted} deleted, {Result.Conflicts.Count} conflicts, {Result.Errors.Count} errors");
From now on, either device can change files and tell the other://After changing files on the pc
await DAG.BroadcastUpdate(Folder.UUID); //the phone syncs by itself
if (!await DAG.CheckIfFolderExists("pc", UUID)) return; //not shared with us
if (await DAG.CheckForUpdate("pc", UUID))
{ var Result = await DAG.SyncFolder("pc", UUID); if (Result.Errors.Count > 0) foreach (var Problem in Result.Errors) Console.WriteLine(Problem);
}
DAG.FolderUpdated += (UUID, From, Result) => Console.WriteLine($"{From} changed {UUID}: {Result.Downloaded} new, {Result.Deleted} deleted, {Result.Conflicts.Count} conflicts"); DAG.Problem += Message => Console.WriteLine("Sync problem: " + Message);
await DAG.StopSharing(Folder.UUID); //this device stops. The files stay where they are
A sync compares three things for every file: this device, the other device, and what both agreed on last time.The conflict name is made from the file's own content, so both devices make the same name and a conflict never multiplies. Both devices end up with the same files.
Safety. A device only gets files from folders it is listed for, and only files that are in the folder's own list. A path another device sends is never used as it is (nothing that climbs out of the folder, nothing in .yuuko, nothing through a shortcut).
A folder that isn't there (an unplugged drive) is an error, not an empty folder, and a sync that would delete nearly everything (more than 10 files and over half) refuses unless AllowMassDelete is on.
Deleted files go to .yuuko/trash/<time>/, never erased. Half-downloaded files wait in .yuuko/partial/. Both are inside the shared folder but never shared.
The first sync of a big folder reads every file once to hash it.
The device names in the Devices list must be the names the other devices call you ("pc", "phone").
Pairing builds the node again: after Identity.NodeRestarted, call DAG.Start(key) again.
Nothing is limited unless you say so (it used to stop at 4000 files and 4 GB per file):DAG.MaxFiles = 100_000; //only if you want a limit
DAG.MaxFileBytes = 20L << 30; //20 GB Many files. The list of files is asked for a page at a time (about 500 KB each), from a list that is kept still while the pages are given, so a folder of any size is listed. If the other device's folder changes between two pages, the list is asked for again from the start (up to 3 times). A list that doesn't move forward, goes back, names a bad path or a bad hash, or has more than your limits, is refused as a whole.
Big files. A file is sent in 256 KB pieces and the places in it are 64-bit, so there is no size at which it stops. A download that stops carries on where it was in a later sync (see below).
Tested with 4100 files syncing between two devices. A file of 4.5 GB was listed, hashed and read at a place past 4 GB, but a whole transfer of a file that big has not been run. Reading and hashing a big file takes as long as the disk takes to read it, on both devices.
Nothing starts a stopped sync again by itself. A sync reports what failed in SyncResult.Errors and carries on with the other files; the next sync fetches only what is still missing, and a file that was half downloaded carries on from the last whole 256 KB piece (it waits in .yuuko/partial/ under its hash, and is checked in full before it is put in place). So your app decides when to try again:var Result = await DAG.ResumeFolder("pc", FolderUUID); //syncs, and while files failed waits a second and syncs again (3 tries)
if (Result.Errors.Count > 0) Console.WriteLine("Still not done: " + Result.Errors[0]); ResumeFolder adds up what the tries downloaded and deleted, and hands back the last try's errors. It throws if the other device can't be reached at all.
The usual places to call it: when a device connects (Identity.YuukoNode.PeerConnected), on a timer, or before you tell the user the folder is up to date (DAG.LastSync[FolderUUID].Errors).
DAG.AutoSync (on by default) starts one sync when a listed device connects or says a folder changed, but doesn't retry it: that is what ResumeFolder is for.
A file that changes on the other device while you download it leaves its old half-copy behind in .yuuko/partial/. Nothing cleans those up yet.

3-reference/8-collective-distribution.ht.title: 8 - Collective Distribution
3-reference/8-collective-distribution.ht.description:
The Cogitarium is the part of Yuuko Protocol where devices near each other pass a signed stream to each other, so one source doesn't have to send it to everyone. It was made specifically for the SCCN (Streaming Gaussian Splatting for High-Density AR), its Collective Distribution part, but it only moves signed bytes, so it works for anything else too. It is also built around a streetpass model: devices that pass each other find each other (Nearby), see what streams are around before accepting any (Offers), and swap small cards (MyCard).Devices in the same chunk (an area) form a mesh. The source signs every piece of the stream and sends it to its best few neighbours. Each device that gets a piece checks the signature, uses it, and passes it to its own best few. With 1000 devices in a room the source only talks to 10 and the rest pass it on, and a device never gets the same piece twice because every piece has a number and repeats are dropped.The five sizes: Cogitarium.Full, ThreeQuarters, Half, Quarter, Sixteenth (the paper's 1, 3/4, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/16). Settings: InitialReceivers (how many the source sends to, default 10), Fanout (how many each device passes it to, default 3), VotesToDistrust (default 3), MaxSegmentBytes (512 KB, cut bigger things up).//On both Cogitarium.Start(); Cogitarium.JoinChunk("district-12"); //On the source: give the others this var Mine = Cogitarium.MyFingerprint; var Stream = Cogitarium.StartStream("district-12", "Cafe scene"); await Stream.Send(FrameBytes, Cogitarium.Full); //signed, and passed along from device to device //On everyone who wants to see it Cogitarium.AcceptSource(FingerprintFromTheSource); //type it, scan it, read it out Cogitarium.SegmentReceived += (Stream, Segment) => Render(Stream.Name, Segment.Level, Segment.Data); A device that doesn't accept the source doesn't keep the stream, doesn't show it and doesn't pass it on. It is only offered to you (its name and who made it, checked against its signature), so you can look at what is around and choose:Cogitarium.StreamOffered += Offer => Console.WriteLine($"{Offer.Name} from {Offer.Fingerprint}"); Cogitarium.Accept(Cogitarium.Offers[0]); //only now it's kept, shown and passed on Offers are never passed on, and only the newest 256 are kept.Cogitarium.Want("district-12", Cogitarium.Quarter, Cogitarium.Sixteenth); //far away: small is enough Cogitarium.Want("district-12"); //nothing listed means every size Devices only send you the sizes you want, and a device that wants only small ones is never sent the big ones.Every device tells its neighbors how it is doing, and the source sends to the best first. The app feeds the numbers in (nothing here measures them):Cogitarium.MyStatus = new Cogitarium.DeviceStatus { WifiStrength = 80, //0 to 100, higher is better WifiUsage = 25, //0 to 100, how busy the wifi has been on average, lower is better BatteryPercent = 70, //0 to 100 BatteryCapacity = 4000, //mAh, how big the battery is }; A neighbor's rank is 0 to 100, higher gets pieces first:rank = (30 x wifi + 15 x (100 - usage) + 25 x battery + 10 x size) / 80, where size is the battery size as a percent of FullCapacity (5000 mAh), minus 30 for every different neighbor that distrusts it. A device that said nothing counts as 50. How fast a device answers is only used to break a tie.The source goes down its list from the best to the worst: it sends to the best InitialReceivers, and a device that refuses or doesn't answer is replaced by the next one down until enough took the piece. Every other device does the same with Fanout for the pieces it passes on. Cogitarium.Neighbors(ChunkID) lists them in that order with each one's Status, Distrusts and Rank.Things to know: The numbers are what the device says. A liar can claim a perfect score and get the pieces first. It still can't change them (they are signed), but it can drop them, and that isn't noticed. The distrust count is not said by the device: each device counts it itself. Reports are checked for range (0 to 100, battery up to 1,000,000 mAh) and anything else is refused. A distrusted device's reports are ignored. A source only has the status of the devices connected to it. In a big mesh each device ranks its own neighbors. Set MyStatus every few seconds at most, not on every change. The rank above is only what a device says. So the devices also rate the main devices, and the source checks them. Mains. The devices the source sends to first (stream.Mains). The source stamps every copy of a piece with the main it sent that copy to, and the stamp travels with it. Rating. Every RateEvery (5 s) each device rates the main that most of its pieces came through: 0 to 100, how many of the pieces that should have come really did. It is sent straight to the source, so a device has to be connected to the source to rate. A main never rates itself. Receipt. A rating carries the number of the newest piece the device holds and a short hash of it. The source remembers what it sent, so it can check: a hash that doesn't match, or a piece the source never sent, is a lie: the device is left out; an old receipt is not a lie: the device is just behind, and it counts as red whatever number it said; so nobody can rate well without really holding the latest pieces. Average and liars. The source averages each main's ratings. If a small group (MinGroup, 3) rates a main very high (HighAt, 90) while at least twice as many rate it very low (LowAt, 30), or the other way round, the group is left out of the average (stream.Suspects(), Cogitarium.Suspected). Nobody is banned: it is decided again every round, so a device that stops lying is counted again. Bouncing. The share of devices that are green (GreenAt, 70) is the stream.Coverage. Under TargetGreen (0.9) the source takes its worst main out and tries the best connection it hasn't tried (or tried the longest ago). If that made it worse, it goes back to the best set it has seen. It repeats until as many devices as possible are green (Cogitarium.MainsChanged). var stream = Cogitarium.StartStream("district-12", "Cafe scene"); Cogitarium.MainsChanged += (Stream, Mains) => Console.WriteLine("now sending to " + string.Join(", ", Mains)); Cogitarium.Suspected += (Stream, Devices) => Console.WriteLine("left out: " + string.Join(", ", Devices)); foreach (var Main in stream.Ratings()) Console.WriteLine($"{Main.Main}: {Main.Mean:0} from {Main.Raters} devices, {Main.Green} green, {Main.Ignored} left out"); Console.WriteLine($"{stream.Coverage:P0} of the devices are green"); Things to know: Free identities still beat it. More fake devices than real ones in the same group will outvote them, because the majority is taken as the truth. A device that received nothing from a main can't blame it. It only rates a main it has pieces from. If everything stopped, Route.Auto is what helps. Devices that aren't connected to the source can't rate. In a big mesh you want every device connected to the source for control (small messages), with the pieces still passed along the mesh. The ratings of a changed set are forgotten, so the new set is rated fresh. A device chooses where its stream comes from:await Cogitarium.SetRoute("district-12", Cogitarium.Route.Internet); //straight from the source await Cogitarium.SetRoute("district-12", Cogitarium.Route.Mesh); //from the other devices (the default) await Cogitarium.SetRoute("district-12", Cogitarium.Route.Auto); //mesh, until nothing has come for AutoAfter (6 s), then internet for AutoRetry (30 s), then mesh again Internet. The source sends every piece to this device itself (it must be connected to it; at most MaxDirect (100) devices). The device tells its neighbors it wants no pieces from them, and stops passing pieces on. It comes back with false and changes nothing if no source of a stream in that chunk can be reached (or the source is full), so a device is never left with nothing. Mesh. The normal way. The source stops sending to this device itself. Auto. Starts as the mesh and switches when pieces stop coming. A device that is on the internet route doesn't rate (there is no main to rate). Every piece is signed by the source, so a device that passes on a changed piece fails the signature at the next device. That device: throws the piece away and distrusts the one that handed it over (no more pieces from it, and it's never used to pass anything on), tells the other devices in the chunk. When enough different neighbours (VotesToDistrust, default 3) say the same about a device, a device distrusts it too, even though it never saw it do anything. The source never picks a distrusted device as one of its first receivers, so the next best one takes its place.Cogitarium.DeviceDistrusted += (Device, Reason) => Console.WriteLine($"{Device}: {Reason}"); Cogitarium.Forgive("tablet"); //if you decide it was a mistake A repeat, a piece for a stream nobody knows, or one that's too big is not tampering: it's refused or ignored, and nobody is blamed. By default it only works between devices that are already connected (your paired group). A normal Yuuko group (group key, pinned devices, mutual TLS) refuses devices it doesn't know. For strangers use Nearby (next section). A device that only drops pieces isn't noticed. Only changing them is. Votes only count from neighbours directly connected to you, but a person with many devices can still vote many times, so don't treat the number as proof. Nothing is sent again to a device that missed a piece. It's for live streams, not files (use 6 - Folder Sync for those). It carries bytes you give it: it doesn't make video or Gaussian splats, it only moves them. Each piece is at most 512 KB. Pairing builds the node again: after Identity.NodeRestarted, call Cogitarium.Start() and join your chunks again. (A running Nearby is not affected by that.) Cogitarium.Start() only works with the devices you paired. For devices you have never met (the streetpass part), call Nearby.Start() instead. It opens a second node next to your private one, with LAN discovery on and its own random identity, and puts Cogitarium on it. Your private group is not touched and still refuses strangers.await Nearby.Start(); //finds devices on the same network by itself await Nearby.Start("nearby.identity"); //a source keeps the same identity every run, so others can keep accepting it await Nearby.Start(null, "tcp/192.168.49.1:7447"); //also call this address right away (e.g. a Wi-Fi Direct group owner) await Nearby.Start(MyTransport); //a link the app built itself (Wi-Fi Aware, a Bluetooth bridge...) as an IYuukoApi Cogitarium.JoinChunk("district-12"); //everything from here is the normal Cogitarium calls Cogitarium.AcceptSource(sourceFingerprint); Nearby.Stop(); //when you leave How it finds them: every few seconds each device announces its ID on the network, and the one with the lower ID calls the other (so only one of the two dials). The handshake is the normal Yuuko one, only without the group key, device list and certificate, because a stranger has none.What a stranger can do on that node: connect, say which chunks it's in, hand over a card, and send stream commands. Every other command is denied, and nothing of your private group is on it. It still can't make you show a stream: you only keep streams from sources you accepted by fingerprint, and every piece is checked against the source's signature.Every device you connect to gets your card and gives you theirs. It is just bytes, so put in whatever the app needs.Nearby.MyCard = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("Herman, likes Gaussian splats"); Nearby.Passed += Met => Console.WriteLine($"{Encoding.UTF8.GetString(Met.Card)} (met {Met.Times} times)"); foreach (var Person in Nearby.People) Console.WriteLine(Person.Fingerprint); The card is whatever they said: nobody checks it. The fingerprint is the part that is checked (it comes from the handshake), so use that to recognise someone you met before. Meeting the same device again within 10 minutes updates its card but isn't another time; later it is (Times goes up and Passed fires again). The list is kept in memory (newest 1000). Save it yourself from Passed if you want it to survive a restart. A new MyCard goes to the devices you connect to from then on. Nearby assumes the devices can already reach each other: the same Wi-Fi, or a Wi-Fi Direct group that the OS has formed (to Zenoh a Wi-Fi Direct group is a network like any other, and devices in it find each other by multicast). If the group owner has a known address, pass it to Start so they call it right away. For a link Zenoh can't use (Wi-Fi Aware, Bluetooth), build it yourself as an IYuukoApi and give it to Nearby.Start(Transport): everything above it (the handshake, the mesh, the cards) is the same.Things to know about Nearby: Forming the Wi-Fi Direct group, or the Bluetooth link, is the app's job (it needs the phone's APIs). Nearby takes it from there. Only the same-network and the given-transport paths are tested. The link under the handshake is not TLS (multicast discovery needs that off), so someone on the network can see who talks to whom, not what. A stranger can make as many identities as it likes, so distrusting one just makes it come back with a new ID, and votes are cheap to fake. It announces a random ID, not your device name and not the one from Identity.CreateNode. You can't run Cogitarium on the private node and on Nearby at the same time: it runs on one. Tested between devices in one process and between two real Zenoh sessions on one machine. Not tested on two physical devices, on a phone, over Wi-Fi Direct, or with many devices.

3-reference/9-audit-log.html.title: 9 - Audit Log
3-reference/9-audit-log.html.description: A small, append-only, tamper-evident record of what a device decided: who connected, who was refused, who was banned, which pairing windows were opened, which group changes were accepted. One file. It can be opened read-only so someone can look without being able to change it.using var audit = AuditLog.Open("audit.log", key); // read + append. One writer at a time. using var recording = audit.Attach(node); // the node's decisions are written down by themselves audit.Append("report.opened", subject: "q3.pdf"); // and your own events using var viewer = AuditLog.OpenReadOnly("audit.log", key); foreach (var e in viewer.Read(kind: "peer.banned")) Console.WriteLine($"{e.TimeUtc} {e.Subject} {e.Detail}"); var result = viewer.Verify(); // result.Ok (or result.BadSeq and result.Problem) audit.Seal(); // done with it: mark the file read-only at the OS level AuditLog.Unseal("audit.log"); // a deliberate step to write again Anything else: audit.Append("your.kind", subject, detail). A kind is letters, digits, ., _, -.Refused connections can come from anybody, so repeats of the same (who, why) within a minute are counted into one entry instead of filling the disk.Each entry contains the hash of the entry before it. Change, remove, add, reorder or repeat an entry and the chain breaks from that point; Verify() names the first bad entry.So use a key for anything that matters. Keep the key out of the same folder as the log. Entries cut off the end, on its own. What remains is still a valid chain. That is what the other devices are for (below), or keep audit.Head yourself and call Verify(expectedHead). Someone who has the key AND the device's own identity, which is the device itself. A signed log (below) can't be forged by anyone else. Deleting the whole file. Reading a missing log is an error, not an empty log. OpenReadOnly can Read and Verify, cannot Append or Attach, and works while the writer is running. Only one writer can have a log open (a second Open fails). A log that ends in a half-written entry, or whose newest entry fails its check, is refused for writing rather than added to. Seal() closes the writer and sets the file read-only (the attribute, and 0444 on Unix). A sealed log refuses to open for writing and says why. It guards against accidents and casual edits, not against someone with the rights to undo it. Every entry is flushed to disk before Append returns. A failure to write (disk full) never reaches the node: see Failures and the AppendFailed event. 1 - Security Overview · 2 - Quickstart · DOGMA VII - The Audit Log · DOGMA III - Event Sourcing (the audit log is a simple tamper-evident record; Event Sourcing is the richer, signed, replicated one that trust levels will be built on)The key stops edits, but whoever holds it can write a whole convincing log, and a chain alone can't see entries cut off the end. Two things fix that.//on the device that writes: every entry is signed with the device's own private key (Dilithium5) using var audit = AuditLog.Open("audit.log", key, signer: Me); //Me is this device's YuukoIdentity using var anchor = audit.AnchorTo(node, "main"); //after every entry, the newest head is sent to the devices we are connected to //on the devices that watch using var witness = new AuditWitness(node, "heads.json", FileKey); //the path and key are optional: without them it is kept in memory //any time later, on the writer or on whoever reads the file var result = await audit.VerifyWithWitnessesAsync(node, "main", expectedSigner: Me.Fingerprint); //result.Ok, result.Problem ("entries were cut off the end", "the log was rewritten"...), result.Witnesses (how many had seen the log) What the others catch: Entries cut off the end: a device saw an entry newer than the last one in the file. A rewritten log: the entry a device saw is not the one in the file at that place (even if the file is now longer), or a device was told two different versions of the same entry. A device that is behind (it saw an older entry that is still in the file) is fine. Things to know: Pass expectedSigner (the fingerprint you pinned when you paired the device). Without it the keys inside the log itself are believed, and a forger with the key writes their own. A witness only knows what it was told. A log written while nobody was connected, or whose watchers were all wiped, can be cut off unnoticed. result.Witnesses tells you how many compared, and 0 means nothing was compared. A witness remembers up to 16 logs per device and ignores anything that isn't a head from that device. The device itself (its identity and its key) could still rewrite its own log from the start, but the devices that saw it will say so.

4-security/1-security-overview.html.description:
How Yuuko keeps your devices' conversations private, in layers. Each layer stops something different, so the later ones still work if an earlier one is beaten.For the exact algorithms and a list of what is tested, see 2 - Security. This page explains how the pieces fit. TLS. The phone and the pc show certificates that come from the same group authority. If either can't, the connection is dropped before any Yuuko message is read. The handshake starts. The phone proves it holds the group key (without sending it), and the pc proves it is the device the phone has pinned, by signing the whole exchange. Keys are made. Both sides work out the same session keys from the group key, fresh random values and two Kyber exchanges. One of those uses a key made for this handshake only and destroyed straight after, so the session can't be opened later even with both devices' identity keys. Everything after that is sealed with AES-256-GCM. A changed or replayed message is rejected. The session is replaced with a fresh handshake after an hour. So the data is protected twice: inside the Yuuko session (device to device) and on the link underneath it (TLS, hop by hop). Pin your devices. If a device isn't pinned, any device that claims its name is accepted. Pairing pins them for you. Set a password on the identity file. Identity.CreateNode has a Password argument that is not used yet, so the identity file is stored without one. Until that is wired up, treat the file as if it were the device itself.
Use a long group key (see 2 - The Group Key) and keep it out of your code and your repo. Check the fingerprint out loud when you pair two devices for the first time. Keep your clocks right. Broadcasts are rejected if the clocks differ by more than a couple of minutes.

4-security/2-the-group-key.html.title: 2 - The Group Key
4-security/2-the-group-key.html.description: The group key is one secret that every device in your group has. It is what makes a Yuuko group a group: a device that doesn't have it can't complete a handshake with the others.In the code it is called the pre-shared key (PreSharedKey, "PSK"). Identity.CreateNode takes it as GroupKey, and turns on RequirePreSharedKey so a device without a long enough one won't start.During every handshake the group key is mixed into the key derivation together with fresh random values and the results of the two Kyber exchanges. It is never sent over the connection. Both devices end up with the same session keys only if they started from the same group key.So a device without the key can still reach the door, but cannot make keys that match, and everything it sends is rejected.When two devices pair, the one-time pairing token is mixed in on top for that one handshake, so only a device that has the pairing code can finish it. It doesn't say which device is which. Every device has the same key, so it can't tell the pc from the phone. That's what the pinned fingerprints are for. It isn't a replacement for pinning. Someone who steals the group key can start handshakes. A device with an allowlist still refuses them, because they aren't pinned. A device without one would accept them. It isn't sent in the pairing code. A new device has to be given the group key separately (type it, scan it, read it out). If you lose it, you can't add devices. It can't be changed on all devices at once yet. If it leaks, every device has to be given a new one by hand and restarted with it. These are two different things that are easy to mix up:Both have to be right for two devices to talk.var Key = Identity.CreateGroupKey(); //16 random characters: the SHORTEST allowed 16 characters is the minimum the library accepts (16 bytes). For anything that matters, make a longer one yourself (32 or more random characters, from a password manager or a random generator) and use the same text on every device. Keep it out of your code, your repo and your logs. Store it the way you'd store a password: encrypted, and only readable by the app. Give it to a new device by hand (type it, show a QR code, read it out). Don't send it over the group's own network before the device is in it. var GroupKey = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(TheGroupKeyText); //the same bytes on every device await Identity.CreateNode(DeviceKey, "pc.id", "pc", true, GroupKey, "pc-devices.json", ListKey); Make a new key. Put it on every device and restart them with it. There is no automatic way to do this yet, and until a device has the new key it can't talk to the others. Unpair any device you don't recognise (Identity.UntrustDevice, Identity.KickDevice with a ban). The audit log (9 - Audit Log) shows connections that were refused, which is one way to notice someone trying.

4-security/3-tls-and-the-link.html.title: 3 - TLS and the Link
4-security/3-tls-and-the-link.html.description:
Yuuko devices talk to each other over Zenoh. TLS and mutual TLS are on by default for that connection. This page explains what that does, what it doesn't, and where the files are.The connection is set up to use TLS 1.3 whenever both devices support it, and to fall back to TLS 1.2 only if one of them can't do 1.3. (That's what the transport's code says it does. I haven't captured a real connection to check which version was used, and it has only been run on one machine.)"Mutual" means both sides show a certificate. Each device has one, signed by the group's certificate authority. A device that can't show a certificate from an authority this device trusts is turned away before a single Yuuko message is read. Hides who talks to whom. On the network, an outsider sees an encrypted connection, not device names, message sizes or timing inside it. Keeps strangers from starting a handshake. The expensive part (the Yuuko handshake) never runs for a device without a certificate. That is the first defence against someone flooding a port. Stops the easy mistakes. With TLS on there is no automatic discovery on the local network, because discovery would have shown a device's presence to anyone. Devices find each other through the address in a pairing code, or addresses you list. It doesn't say which device is which. The certificate says "a member of this group". What proves a device is the one you pinned is the Yuuko handshake and its fingerprints. It isn't what protects your data. TLS only covers one hop, between two neighbouring devices. The messages are sealed again by the Yuuko handshake (AES-256-GCM, with a fresh throw-away key) from device to device, so the data is encrypted twice. If TLS were broken, the Yuuko layer is still there. If a device relays a broadcast, it can read it and can't change it (see 1 - Security Overview).
It doesn't make the group key unnecessary. See 2 - The Group Key. The first device's certificate authority becomes the group's. When a device pairs, the one that offered the pairing hands over the authority (certificate and key) over the encrypted session, and the newcomer makes itself a certificate from it. From then on everyone trusts the same single authority, so adding a device never means updating the others and nobody has to restart. Because every member holds the authority's key, a stolen member could make certificates. That only gets someone past the TLS layer. The handshake still has to succeed, and removing a device from the group (Identity.UntrustDevice, KickDevice) is how you shut it out. A device that already has paired devices of its own will not leave them to join a different group. It refuses. Mutual TLS would turn a newcomer away, so the pairing code carries a temporary certificate for it alone, valid for the pairing window plus two minutes. After pairing the newcomer has to open its connection again to switch to its permanent one (Identity.ConnectToDevice builds the node again for this, but that hasn't been tried over a real network yet). Until then it uses the temporary one, which stops being accepted for new connections after a few minutes.The pairing code carries that temporary certificate and its key, so treat the code as a secret until it is used or expires. Anyone who sees it (a shoulder-surfed screen, a photo) can pair in that window.%LOCALAPPDATA%/YuukoProtocol/tls/<device name> (or the folder you set as TlsDirectory): Zenoh needs the keys as files, so they are plain PEM, not password-protected. Anyone who copies one can pretend to be that device at the TLS layer only. They still can't pass the handshake. On Linux the folder is made owner-only; on Windows it sits under your profile, so protect your profile. A device's trust list is read when the connection opens. It changes when the device joins a group while pairing, or when you call YuukoTls.TrustPeer yourself. YuukoTls.Check(folder, name) tells you the state of a device's certificates without changing anything: Missing, Valid, ExpiresSoon, Expired or Invalid. You can (EnableTls = false). Then LAN auto-discovery comes back and the connection's metadata (who talks to whom, sizes, timing) is visible to anyone on the network. The messages themselves are still sealed by the Yuuko handshake. There is rarely a reason to do this outside a test.If you don't name a port, the transport listens on the first free port from 7447 and tells you which (transport.ListenEndpoints). Make sure your firewall lets the app through; the pairing code carries the address.
